findings.headline: Your headline says you charge for work done. Scheduling alone is billable.
findings.explanation: A therapist who schedules 40 appointments and writes 20 notes pays for 40.

claim_a.statement: Charges for jobs done, not access
claim_a.quote: Legacy EHRs charge for access. We charge for jobs done.

claim_b.statement: Billable on scheduling, note or not
claim_b.quote: A session is counted each time you generate an AI note or schedule a session with a client

findings.why_not_just_wording: Scheduling is access, which is the thing the headline says you do not charge for.
findings.caveat: The $69 monthly cap limits the damage, and the same answer explains that the fee covers the whole platform.

findings.headline: Free claims offer is advertised to everyone, restricted to solo practices in one line.
findings.explanation: Group practices submit the most claims and are the ones budgeting on the wrong number.

claim_a.statement: $0.30 per claim, free till end of September
claim_a.quote: $0.30 per claim submission, $0.15 per eligibility check

findings.why_not_just_wording: Three places state the offer with no restriction and one place limits it to a subset of customers.
findings.caveat: Four words on the pricing page would fix it. The restriction line also contains a typo, so it looks like a late addition.

findings.headline: Trial is 30 days on the pricing page, 14 days on the pricing reference.
findings.explanation: A practice manager comparing tools gets two answers depending on which page they land on.
findings.why_not_just_wording: Both pages present their number as the trial a team would get.
findings.caveat: The 14-day figure sits on a page headed Legacy plans, so it may be out of date. Nothing on the page marks where legacy ends.

findings.headline: Canadian page prices card fees in C$ and claim fees in US$.
findings.explanation: A Canadian customer cannot tell whether a claim costs C$0.30 or about C$0.41.

claim_a.quote: Low fees for card transactions: 2.9% + C$0.30

claim_b.quote: $0.30 per claim submission, $0.15 per eligibility check

findings.why_not_just_wording: The page converts every other price on it, so a bare dollar sign reads as a different currency.
findings.caveat: Looks like a localisation pass that missed the insurance billing block.

findings.headline: Premium is both your current tier and a discontinued $99 plan.
findings.explanation: A prospect searching for the price of Premium finds $99, $69, or $1 per session capped at $69.

claim_a.quote: you won't be able to use features only included in our Premium plan

findings.why_not_just_wording: One plan name carries two prices and two billing models.
findings.caveat: Your FAQ says outright that pricing changed and links to the legacy page, which is more than most companies do.

findings.headline: One offer names a month that has passed. Another names no year.
findings.explanation: A reader cannot tell from either page whether the offer is still open.
findings.why_not_just_wording: Both are statements about when an offer applies, and neither resolves to a date a reader can act on.
findings.caveat: The beta may have opened on time and the wording simply not been updated.

coverage_notes.what_was_not_checkable: Your support centre could not be read. Every collection page returned only its title and a few links because the content is built in the browser, so no help article was checked against the pricing page. upheal.io/terms returns a 404 from our crawl, so renewal, refund and price-change terms were not reviewed. The Group and Custom Enterprise plans publish no prices, so team pricing could not be checked. The plan comparison tables are built from styled divs rather than real tables, so per-plan values lose their column alignment when flattened to text. Nothing above depends on reading them.
